title: The Curé of Ars (1786–1859)
hook: a struggling student priest who, his biographers say, came to spend up to sixteen hours a day hearing confessions

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Church that is always being called to renewal, perennis reformatio. Your line was always renewing. What did you start over on? Today a new stretch of the long story begins: the modern Church, and a village priest. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

A seminary classroom in France, and one student cannot get the Latin to stay in his head. The lectures are in Latin. The exams are in Latin. He is older than the others, a farmer's son, and he fails. A local priest takes him on as a private pupil and keeps him going, more out of trust than results. In the end he is ordained, and the Church sends him to a small, quiet village called Ars. His biographers remember the vicar general telling him there was not much love of God in that parish, and that he would put some there. Within his lifetime, people were coming to that village from far away, waiting in line for hours, sometimes for days. They were not coming for his Latin. They were coming to kneel in a small wooden box and talk to him.
screen: `A STUDENT WHO FAILS THE LATIN.` → `SENT TO A SMALL VILLAGE.` → `CROWDS COME TO ARS.`

segments.voice: His name was Jean-Marie Vianney, and Catholics know him as the Curé of Ars. Curé is simply the French word for a parish priest. First, the slow start. He was no scholar, and he knew it. What he had was stubbornness and prayer. He spent long hours in his church, and he went from house to house getting to know the farm families of the village. Second, the box. The confessional is where a Catholic tells a priest their sins and hears the words of absolution, forgiveness given in God's name. The Curé's early biographers say that in his later years he sat there up to sixteen hours a day. Tradition says he slept little and ate plainly so he could keep going. People came because they said he listened, and because he seemed to understand them. Third, a farmer in the back pew. A story told about him: he noticed an old man who sat in the church for long stretches without moving his lips. Asked what he did there, the man answered, as the story goes, that he looked at God and God looked at him. The Curé loved that answer, and repeated it. Fourth, why it matters. The Church later named him patron of parish priests. Not of brilliant priests. Of ordinary ones in ordinary places. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells a story of a shepherd who leaves the flock to find one lost sheep, and says there shall be joy in heaven "upon one sinner that doth penance." One. The Curé of Ars spent his life on the one in front of him.
screen: `A SLOW START, A STUBBORN PRAYER.` · `THE BOX: SIXTEEN HOURS A DAY.` · `I LOOK AT HIM, HE LOOKS AT ME.` · `PATRON OF ORDINARY PRIESTS.` · then, large: `UPON ONE SINNER THAT DOTH PENANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Many Catholics take a day like this as a nudge toward confession. Whatever your path, the two minutes are the same. Settle, and breathe. Let one thing surface that you would rather not look at: a word you said, a thing you left undone. Don't argue with it. Just name it, quietly, to yourself. If that nudge is yours, you might look up when your parish hears confessions. If you pray, you can bring that one thing to God. If you don't, simply let it be seen, and breathe out. The bell holds the time.
Confessional. The small wooden box where Jean-Marie Vianney, the Curé of Ars, sat hearing confessions and giving absolution, up to sixteen hours a day.
Your line: sixteen hours a day. Today, give one person your full, unhurried attention, the way he gave it to the people who knelt in that box. Day eight hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics go to confession, the sacrament of penance, at their parish, often on Saturdays or before Mass; many parishes add extra hours in Lent and Advent, and priests keep the Curé of Ars's feast on August 4.
